function.name: give_up
function.arguments: {"reason": "Arithmetic exhaustion of the 900-step budget, not loss of the object. 763 control steps are spent and 137 remain. The block is now ~6 cm off in -x from the hand (measured eef 0.0192, 0.0312, 0.8938; block at about x=-0.04, y=+0.03) and the bowl a further ~15 cm in +x. Finishing needs reposition 6 cm + descent 7 cm + close + lift 10 cm + traverse 15 cm + release, i.e. roughly 45 cm of Cartesian travel, but this rig servo advances only ~1-1.5 mm per control step, so ~450 steps are required against 137 available. Three closes at z=0.90, 0.881 and 0.894 all returned the fully-closed reading 0.0162, so nothing is grasped and the block is still on the table.", "hindsight": "RIG FACTS worth more than the failed attempt. (1) STEP ACCOUNTING IS THE REAL CONSTRAINT: the number of control steps a move_to executes is set by the largest normalised dimension change - positions ~0.04 m/step, gripper ~0.0125/step, yaw ~0.3 rad/step. A pure 8 cm position command therefore buys only 2-3 steps and moves the arm a few mm, while toggling the gripper 0<->1 buys ~80 steps. Plan every long translation around a gripper toggle, and remember the toggle must land on the state you want. (2) The Cartesian servo lags at ~1-1.6 mm per control step, so budget ~100 steps per 10 cm of travel and count the total against 900 before choosing approach heights; my descent profile (1.00 -> 0.93 -> 0.906 -> 0.881 -> 1.005 -> 0.894) burned ~600 steps on vertical re-approaches. (3) Fingertips sit ~6.5 cm below eef_pos: at eef z=0.90 the pads are level with the top of a ~3.5 cm block and close on air; grasp a block on the 0.80 m table at eef z~0.87-0.88. (4) measured gripper 0.016 = jaws touching each other = missed; an intermediate value (~0.3-0.5) is the only evidence of actually holding. (5) THE BOWL CONTAINS A SMALL RED DOT AT ITS CENTRE (a goal marker). From the wrist camera at low altitude it is the only red thing in frame and is trivially mistaken for the target block - check apparent size and context before steering at it. (6) The fixed front and side cameras are useless for localising along world x: a 13.7 cm x translation of the hand changed its image column by under 10 px in both views, so treat them as y/height references only. The wrist camera is the only usable x sensor, via parallax: fit the block image row against measured eef x (about 450 px/m at 15-20 cm standoff) rather than trying to read absolute positions. (7) The wrist camera axes are rotated relative to the arm: at yaw~0.05 image-up is roughly +x; rotating yaw by exactly pi/2 maps image-up to image-right, which is a cheap, grasp-neutral way (square block, jaws symmetric about the TCP) to disambiguate the axes - do that early, not at call 11. (8) Descending or closing inside the block column with the jaws open sweeps the block sideways; once it has been knocked, all earlier position estimates are void and must be re-derived from a high vantage (z~1.0) where the wrist camera sees the block and the bowl in the same frame. (9) Best sequence for this task given the budget: one call to hover above the block from a high vantage, one call to open+descend to z=0.875, one call to close, then lift only 3-4 cm (enough to clear the table) and go straight at the bowl in a single interpolated line, releasing by commanding gripper 1 while hovering above the rim."}
